rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from mentioning God in the third person to direct-address pronouns turns the setting into one of witnessed presence and speech.
rows.anchor: صار مقام الغيبة مقام مشاهدة فناسب أن يغير الإضمار إلى ضمائر المشاهدة وهو مقام التكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical shift hints that at al-Aqsa the Prophet moved from reasoning about the unseen to entering the realm of vision.
rows.anchor: قد انتقل من مقام الاستدلال على عالم الغيب إلى مقام مصيره في عالم المشاهدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift prepares for the pronoun in “He is the Hearing, Seeing,” whose apparent antecedent differs from the pronoun in “We showed him”; nearby return after an iltifat is less elegant.
rows.anchor: لأن الشأن تناسق الضمائر ، ولأن العود إلى الالتفات بالقرب ليس من الأحسن

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators take both pronouns in “He is the Hearing, Seeing” to refer to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: عائدان إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وقاله بعض المفسرين

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi considers the Prophet a likely antecedent for the two pronouns.
rows.anchor: الأظهر أن الضميرين عائدان إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وقاله بعض المفسرين ، واستقربه الطيبي

rows.speaker: جمهرة المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators instead take the pronouns to refer to God.
rows.anchor: ولكن جمهرة المفسرين على أنه عائد إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording may intentionally sustain both readings, since the Quran can invite meanings suited to different levels of understanding.
rows.anchor: وقد تجيء الآيات محتملة عدة معانن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The separated sentence’s “inna” is emphatic and causal; it explains either the assignment of showing to its agent or its attachment to its recipient as wise giving to the worthy.
rows.anchor: التوكيد والتعليل كما يؤذن به فصل الجملة عما قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The causal reading is stronger if the pronoun means the Prophet, since the extraordinary vision was given to someone the polytheists doubted could bear it.
rows.anchor: وإنما المحتاج للتعليل هو إعطاء تلك الإراءة العجيبة لمن شك المشركون في حصولها له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic restriction casts the Prophet as the one who truly perceived what he heard and saw, rebutting claims that he lied or imagined it; this favors the Prophetic antecedent.
rows.anchor: أي هو المدرك لما سمعه وأبصره لا الكاذب ولا المتوهم كما زعم المشركون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence about Moses is a new clause coordinated with the opening glorification: God took Muhammad on the journey and gave Moses the Book, two immense favors to humanity.
rows.anchor: فهما منتان عظيمتان على جزء عظيم من البشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mention of al-Aqsa leads to Israel’s history there as an example for Muslims to emulate or heed as their fortunes rise and fall.
rows.anchor: فإن أطوار المسجد الأقصى تمثل ما تطور به حال بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s being shown signs makes the gift of the Quran an implied parallel to the Torah given to Moses; verse 9 calls the Quran’s guidance straighter, though both books guide.
rows.anchor: فإن من آيات الله التي أوتيها النبي آية القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night journey parallels Moses receiving prophecy by night while travelling with his family from Midian after seeing a fire at the Mount, and his later ascent to converse with God.
rows.anchor: فقد أوتي النبوءة ليلا وهو سار بأهله من أرض مدين إذ آنس من جانب الطور نارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The Book” is the familiar Torah, and its pronoun refers to that book; calling it guidance makes the means of guidance stand for guidance itself.
rows.anchor: والكتاب هو المعهود إيتاؤه موسى عليه السلام وهو التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel is singled out because the Torah’s law addressed them; “people” can mean a subset, while others may still benefit from the Torah’s guidance.
rows.anchor: وخص بني إسرائيل لأنهم المخاطبون بشريعة التوراة دون غيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “guidance for people” can refer to Israel in particular, and a scripture addressed to one people can benefit others as well.
rows.anchor: لأن الناس قد يطلق على بعضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Descendants” may be an aside at the end of the reported address, in the accusative of specification, clarifying Israel while reproaching their ingratitude.
rows.anchor: لزيادة بيان بني إسرائيل بيانا مقصودا به التعريض بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively it completes the explanatory address as “being descendants,” or is a vocative with an omitted call, urging gratitude and avoidance of shirk.
rows.anchor: أي حال كونكم ذرية من حملنا مع نوح عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Carrying” means placing something on something else for transport; here it means the ark and the ancestors rescued with Noah from the flood.
rows.anchor: أي ذرية من أنجيناهم من الطوفان مع نوح عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s gratitude explains the ban on taking another protector: ancestors were saved by God, and Noah and his companions were grateful, so Israel should follow them.
rows.anchor: لأن أجدادهم حملوا مع نوح بنعمة من الله عليهم لنجاتهم من الغرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gratitude sentence may remain part of the explanation addressed to Israel, or be a tailpiece to the account of Moses’s Book addressing Quran followers.
rows.anchor: فيكون خطابا لأهل القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel descends from Shem, one of those aboard the ark; saying “descendants of those We carried” rather than “Noah’s descendants” recalls the blessing of rescue.
rows.anchor: لأن بني إسرائيل من ذرية سام بن نوح وكان سام ممن ركب السفينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recalling that Noah and his companions were saved through gratitude urges imitation and warns that associating partners risks a destructive punishment.
rows.anchor: أن الله أنجى نوحا ومن معه من الهلاك بسبب شكره وشكرهم تحريضا على الائتساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s descendants split into the obedient rescued with him and his arrogant, unbelieving son who drowned; Israel descends from the righteous branch and must imitate it to survive.
rows.anchor: وكان بنو إسرائيل من ذرية الفريق البار ، فإن اقتدوا به نجوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah represents two lineages, making him a better comparison than Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob; Israel’s two later devastations answer their failure to keep faith with the promise associated with Noah’s rescue.
rows.anchor: وهذا التماثل هو نكتة اختيار ذكر نوح من بين أجدادهم الآخرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic “indeed” treats Israel as if unaware of Noah’s gratitude, either to press them to imitate him or to expose Arab polytheists by analogy.
rows.anchor: إما لتوثيق حملهم على الاقتداء به إن كانت الجملة خطابا لبني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A servant is one who acknowledges servitude to God without the arrogance of shirk; “grateful” means intensely thanking God through obedience.
rows.anchor: أنه معترف لله بالعبودية غير متكبر بالإشراك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unspecified report says Noah used to praise God frequently.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه كان يكثر حمد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nations naturally prize emulating virtuous ancestors, and departure from that model can cast doubt on the claimed lineage.
rows.anchor: والاقتداء بصالح الآباء مجبولة عليه النفوس ومحل تنافس عند الأمم

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nabigha’s verse treats Noah as the model of keeping trust, showing Arabs knew and could imitate him.
rows.anchor: كذلك كان نوح لا يخون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following warning explains God’s decree to Israel; its second-person address rules out construing “the Book” as the Preserved Tablet or merely God’s knowledge.
rows.anchor: ضمائر الخطاب في هذه الجملة مانعة من أن يكون المراد بالكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two periods encompass two series of conflicts: Israel’s wars with the Babylonians and later with the Romans, each containing multiple campaigns.
rows.anchor: حوادث عظيمة بين بني إسرائيل وأعدائهم من أمتين عظيمتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first period is the Babylonian captivity: Nebuchadnezzar invaded Jerusalem in 606 BCE, again more severely in 598 BCE, then in 588 BCE deported Judah, burned Solomon’s Temple, and left Jerusalem ruined.
rows.anchor: الأسر البابلي وهي غزوات ( بختنصر ) ملك بابل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second period is Rome’s succession of invasions in Jerusalem, to be explained at the later promise of the second period.
rows.anchor: وأما المرة الثانية فهي سلسلة غزوات الرومانيين بلاد أورشليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wrongdoing is ascribed to Israel collectively because most of the community was corrupt, though it still contained righteous people.
rows.anchor: إسناد الإفساد إلى ضمير بني إسرائيل مفيد أنه إفساد من جمهورهم بحيث تعد الأمة كلها مفسدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Rising high” metaphorically means tyranny and disobedience, likening an abstract moral offense to physically towering over something.
rows.anchor: مجاز في الطغيان والعصيان كقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The underlying forms of both verbs include a doubled emphatic ending: “you will surely corrupt” and “you will surely rise high.”
rows.anchor: وأصل { لتفسدن } لتفسدونن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Promise” means the promised event or appointed time, as in God’s promise to make the barrier level.
rows.anchor: أي الزمان المقدر لحصول المرة الأولى من الإفساد والعلو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A promise fulfilled” means a promise carried out and executed.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك قوله : وكان وعدا مفعولا } أي معمولا ومنفذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first of the two promises is an explanatory attribution: the appointed event belonging to the first corruption and rebellion.
rows.anchor: وإضافة { وعد } إلى { أولاهما } بيانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sending the armies means causing their march and arranging its circumstances by creation and subjection, not by revelation or a divine command.
rows.anchor: وهو بعث تكوين وتسخير لا بعث بوحي وأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition “upon” conveys domination, like its use in the promise to send tormentors against Israel.
rows.anchor: وتعدية بعثنا } بحرف الاستعلاء لتضمينه معنى التسليط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “servants” are mortal subjects, specifically the Assyrians of Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar’s troops; the term is commonly used with “of God,” while unqualified “slaves” is عبيد.
rows.anchor: والمقصود بعباد الله هنا الأشوريون أهل بابل وهم جنود بختنصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Might” means force and severity in war; calling it severe signals strength in its kind.
rows.anchor: والبأس : الشوكة والشدة في الحرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The raiding clause coordinates with the sending and belongs to the decree; جوس means moving repeatedly through a land to investigate it, here pursuing combatants destructively.
rows.anchor: والجوس : التخلل في البلاد وطرقها ذهابا وإيابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Through the dwellings” refers to Jerusalem’s houses, which Nebuchadnezzar’s troops entered, destroyed, and burned along with the Temple, taking Israel into captivity.
rows.anchor: وهي ديار بلد أورشليم فقد دخلها جيش بختنصر وقتل الرجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The dwellings” also includes Solomon’s Temple, Israel’s place of worship; the next verse’s entry into the mosque corroborates this reading.
rows.anchor: ولفظ ( الديار ) يشمل هيكل سليمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return of victory continues the answer to the first promise and remains part of the decree; past tense after “when” assures a future event.
rows.anchor: وهو ماض لفظا مستقبل معنى ، لأن ( إذا ) ظرف لما يستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then” marks both chronological delay and a higher rank in the sequence.
rows.anchor: و ( ثم ) تفيد التراخي الرتبي والتراخي الزمني معا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Victory returned to you” means returning to the place from which they had gone; “against them” describes that return as a circumstance.
rows.anchor: والكرة : الرجعة إلى المكان الذي ذهب منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After more than forty years in exile and repentance, Persian kings weakened Babylon: Cyrus fought it, Darius captured it in 538 BCE, and in 530 BCE Jews were allowed to return to Jerusalem and restore their state.
rows.anchor: ثم نزل بهم ( داريوس ) ملك فارس وفتح بابل سنة 538 قبل المسيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return counted as Israel’s victory because they helped the Persians defeat Babylon.
rows.anchor: وذلك نصر انتصروه على البابليين إذ كانوا أعوانا للفرس عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised Persian victory also appears in Isaiah’s tenth through twelfth chapters and Jeremiah’s twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth.
rows.anchor: والوعد بهذا النصر ورد أيضا في كتاب أشعياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth, children, and population were among the promised favors, reflected in Jeremiah’s instruction to the exiles to build homes, plant gardens, marry, and grow in number.
rows.anchor: خذوا نساء ولدوا بنين وبناتت ، واكثروا هناك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafīr is a collective noun for a person’s kin and tribe who go out with him; “more numerous” is specified by it.
rows.anchor: والنفير . اسم جمع للجماعة التي تنفر مع المرء من قومه وعشيرته

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: Abu Jahl’s phrase “neither in the caravan nor in the group” illustrates the collective sense of نفير.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول أبي جهل : ( لا في العير ولا في النفير )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “More numerous” most likely compares Israel to themselves before exile, fitting the context of favor; some commentators compare them with their Babylonian enemies instead.
rows.anchor: أي جعلناكم أكثر مما كنتم قبل الجلاء

rows.speaker: جمع من المفسرين
rows.claim: A group of commentators say Israel outnumbered the Babylonians after most Babylonians died in wars with Persia.
rows.anchor: وقال جمع من المفسرين : أكثر نفيرا من أعدائكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exhortation is part of the decree addressed to Israel and echoes Jeremiah’s counsel to seek the city’s peace, since their peace depended on its peace.
rows.anchor: وهو حكاية لما في الإصحاح التاسع والعشرين من كتاب أرميا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel’s renewed success followed repentance and a new generation; good action benefits its doer, while wrongdoing brings the fate of earlier generations.
rows.anchor: نرد لكم الكرة لأجل التوبة وتجدد الجيل وقد أصبحتم في حالة نعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “you do good” gives the act special emphasis rather than saying only that good is for yourselves.
rows.anchor: وإعادة فعل { أحسنتم } تنويه فلم يقل : إن أحسنتم فلأنفسكم

rows.speaker: الأحوص
rows.claim: Al-Ahwas’s verse repeats the same verb form, serving as a poetic parallel for the Quranic construction.
rows.anchor: فإذا تزول تزول عن متخمط تخشى بوادره على الأقران

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni says repeating a verb is licensed when the second instance takes a prepositional complement that supplies its point, as in the cited verse and the Quranic example.
rows.anchor: لما اتصل بالفعل الثاني من حرف الجر المفادة منه الفائدة

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali resisted Ibn Jinni’s reading of the Quranic example because the second verb could instead be emphatic and what follows a new explanation.
rows.anchor: أنه يرى جواز أن تكون أغويناهم تأكيدا لأغوينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author's view is that Abu Ali’s objection reflects the Quranic example’s ambiguity; Ibn Jinni’s explanation is definite in the poem and the simple illustrative sentence.
rows.anchor: غير أن الأمر فيها عندي على ما عرفتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating a verb to attach a new complement is elegant Arabic that draws attention to the act, as in two other Quranic passages.
rows.anchor: وأسلوب إعادة الفعل عند إرادة تعلق شيء به أسلوب عربي فصيح يقصد به الاهتمام بذلك الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction uses tajrīd: it treats the doer’s own self as someone for whom he acts, and the lām is the verb’s complement.
rows.anchor: بأن جعلت نفس المحسن كذات يحسن لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “if you do wrong, then for it,” an omitted verb means “you do wrong for it”; this is verbal government with lām, unlike the nominal predicate construction in 41:46.
rows.anchor: قوله : { فلها } متعلق بفعل محذوف بعد فاء الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 41:46 has no tajrīd: a nominal “his good is for himself, his wrong upon him” makes the prepositional phrases predicates, whereas this verse’s verbs take lām.
rows.anchor: أن آية فصلت ليس فيها تجريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fā’ in “when the later promise comes” marks a consequence of wrongdoing, efficiently linking the second period to the earlier division and showing that misconduct brings it about.
rows.anchor: وقد حصل بهذا التفريع إيجاز بديع قضاء لحق التقسيم الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The later” modifies an omitted noun, “the second promise,” inferred from the mention of two periods.
rows.anchor: دل عليه قوله : { مرتين } ، أي وعد المرة الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The continuation remains part of what was decreed in the Book, as shown by its causal fā’.
rows.anchor: وهذا الكلام من بقية ما قضي في الكتاب بدليل تفريعه بالفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later period is the opposite of the first; the following lām clauses express purpose, since the well-known readings keep their second and third lām vowelled rather than jussive.
rows.anchor: ولامات ( ليسوؤوا ، وليدخلوا ، وليتبروا ) للتعليل

rows.speaker: نافع، ابن كثير، أبو عمرو، حفص، أبو جعفر، يعقوب
rows.claim: These readers use plural ليسوؤوا, matching the other plural verbs; its unspoken agents are supplied from the “We sent servants” construction.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع ، وابن كثير ، وأبو عمرو ، وحفص ، وأبو جعفر ، ويعقوب { ليسوؤا } بضمير الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural agents are not the same people who raided first, since history and commentators identify a different nation in the later event.
rows.anchor: حسب شهادة التاريخ وأقوال المفسرين كما سيأتي

rows.speaker: ابن عامر، حمزة، أبو بكر عن عاصم، خلف
rows.claim: These readers have the singular “to cause sorrow,” with God as subject; al-Kisa’i instead reads “that We cause sorrow” in the divine plural.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر ، وحمزة ، وأبو بكر عن عاصم ، وخلف ليسوء

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa’i reads نسوء in the first-person plural, while the other cited singular readers refer to God in third person.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكسائي { لنسوء } بنون العظمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The written form permits either the plural reading, with alif as the separator, or the singular forms, with alif marking hamza.
rows.anchor: فالرسم يسمح بقراءة واو الجماعة على أن يكون الألف ألف الفرق وبقراءتي الإفراد على أن الألف علامة الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They cause sorrow and enter” refers back to the servants by the noun’s grammatical form, not its later historical referent; “as they entered the first time” refers to the earlier invaders.
rows.anchor: وضميرا ( ليسوءوا وليدخلوا ) عائدان إلى { عبادا لنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waw in “if you return, We return” may coordinate a warning after the promise of mercy, or introduce a parenthetic threat.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن تكون الواو عاطفة على جملة { عسى ربكم أن يرحمكم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mercy and safety in the lands where they seek refuge, returning to corruption would bring a repetition of worldly punishment.
rows.anchor: والمعنى : بعد أن يرحمكم ربكم ويؤمنكم في البلاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hell sentence adds the afterlife punishment to the worldly punishments just described, and its general wording includes the addressees and other unbelievers.
rows.anchor: لإفادة أن ما ذكر قبله من عقاب إنما هو عقاب دنيوي وأن وراءه عقاب الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning makes worldly punishment depend on corruption and violating the law; the later generation also disbelieved Jesus, while the earlier one killed prophets including Isaiah and Jeremiah.
rows.anchor: عقابهم في الدنيا ليس مقصورا على ذنوب الكفر بل هو منوط بالإفساد في الأرض وتعدي حدود الشريعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaṣīr is a place from which escape is impossible, either with the active sense “confining” or the passive sense “confined in.”
rows.anchor: والحصير : المكان الذي يحصر فيه فلا يستطاع الخروج منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This Quran” points to the portion already revealed and mentally present to people, and the demonstrative underscores its importance.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى الحاضر في أذهان الناس من المقدار المنزل من القرآن قبل هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse consoles believers after Israel’s frightening history: Quranic guidance can protect them from Israel’s fate, and the Quran customarily follows warning with hope or the reverse.
rows.anchor: فأخبروا بأن في القرآن ما يعصمهم عن الوقوع فيما وقع فيه بنو إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The one that is straighter” omits a noun such as path or religion, understood from guidance; the omission is concise and ennobling.
rows.anchor: لأن الهداية من ملازمات السير والطريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran guides to a way straighter than the Torah’s guidance, with an assurance that its community can remain on that way.
rows.anchor: ففيه إيماء إلى ضمان سلامة أمة القرآن من الحيدة عن الطريق الأقوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic guidance uses comprehensive, accessible encouragement and warning; its superiority concerns the means of reaching truth, not truth itself, and its treatment of shirk avoids confusing human reverence with divine praise.
rows.anchor: بحيث لا يعدم المتدبر في معانيه اجتناء ثمار أفنانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reward and punishment may mean Paradise and Hell, but the broader reading includes worldly reward and torment and fits the contrast between Israel’s prosperity and suffering.
rows.anchor: فيشمل أجر الدنيا وعذابها ، وهو المناسب لما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who disbelieve in the Hereafter are Quraysh, enemies of the believers; announcing their punishment counts as glad tidings to their opponents.
rows.anchor: إذ المراد بالذين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة مشركو قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only believers and Quraysh disbelievers are mentioned because the immediate issue is the polytheists’ denial of the night journey, not the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: والاقتصار على هذين الفريقين هو مقتضى المقام لمناسبة تكذيب المشركين بالإسراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the verse’s placement and wording are obscure, the author links it to disbelievers mocking the warning and asking when its promised judgment will arrive.
rows.anchor: ولم يأت فيها المفسرون بما ينثلج له الصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement answers the mockery by reminding hearers that the threatened promise has an appointed time; “the human” here means the unbeliever, a common Quranic usage.
rows.anchor: فالمراد بالإنسان الإنسان الذي لا يؤمن بالآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “calls” means seeking or asking for something, as shown by Labid’s poetic usage.
rows.anchor: مستعمل في معنى يطلب ويبتغي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal noun compares haste for evil with haste for good: the unbeliever impatiently asks when a threat will come as someone impatiently awaits promised benefit.
rows.anchor: أي يستعجل الشر كاستعجاله الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concluding “the human is hasty” generalizes to the human kind, including these unbelievers; kāna marks an established trait, as in another Quranic description.
rows.anchor: فالإنسان هنا مراد به الجنس لأنه المناسب للتذييل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The point is their lack of foresight: God times events wisely and gradually brings both good and evil, rather than granting impatient requests.
rows.anchor: الكناية عن عدم تبصره وأن الله أعلم بمقتضى الحكمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bā’ may reinforce the close link between verb and object, or دعاء may imply hastening, as in “those who do not believe in it hasten it.”
rows.anchor: لتأكيد لصوق العامل بمعموله كالتي في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAjūl is an intensive form of ʿājil, “hasty.”
rows.anchor: وعجول : صيغة مبالغة في عاجل . يقال : عجل فهو عاجل وعجول .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The written form omits the wāw in يدع to reflect connected pronunciation; al-Farrā’ says writing it with wāw would also be correct.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : لو كتبت بالواو لكان صوابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The link is that haste cannot alter an appointed term; since terms are spans of time, night and day illustrate their passing.
rows.anchor: وهذا شائع عند الناس في أن الزمان متقض وإن طال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day are signs of the Creator’s existence and power and favors to people; day enables travel, while night’s rest is implied by the contrast, and alternating light permits counting years.
rows.anchor: وهو كونهما آيتين على وجود الصانع وعظيم القدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their opposition also illustrates disbelief and belief, misguidance and guidance, tying the night-day image to the Torah, Quranic guidance, warning, and individual accountability; this layered compression exemplifies Quranic rhetoric.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا بعد ذلك كله إيماء إلى ضرب مثل للكفر والإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fā’ clause about erasing night is an inserted parenthesis between the creation statement and its purpose clause.
rows.anchor: وتفريع جملة فمحونا آية الليل } اعتراض وقع بالفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Sign of night/day” may mean night and day themselves, or their associated moon and sun; on the latter reading the moon’s light is reflected sunlight and the sun makes things visible, an especially precise reading.
rows.anchor: ومعنى كون آية النهار مبصرة أن الشمس جعل ضوؤها سبب إبصار الناس الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Erasing means extinguishing light; darkness hides objects, while “seeing day” attributes vision to its cause by rational metaphor.
rows.anchor: لأن النور يظهر الأشياء والظلمة لا تظهر فيها الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reason for seeking God’s bounty is attached particularly to daylight, whose benefit is more evident; recognizing it also makes one recognize the night’s rest.
rows.anchor: وجاء التعليل لحكمة آية النهار خاصة دون ما يقابلها من حكمة الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both signs also make years countable; this is clearest with night because most people measure months and years by lunar nights.
rows.anchor: لأن جمهور البشر يضبط الشهور والسنين بالليالي ، أي حساب القمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Calculation” generalizes beyond the specific mention of years to days, months, and seasons.
rows.anchor: والحساب يشمل حساب الأيام والشهور والفصول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concluding statement that everything is detailed reinforces that every appointed term has a known measure, unaffected by impatience or delay.
rows.anchor: أن الله قد جعل لكل شيء قدرا لا إبهام فيه ولا شك عنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafṣīl means clarifying and distinguishing, from separation; divine detail includes creation, order, and knowledge, while what is revealed to people is only part of it.
rows.anchor: التبيين والتمييز وهو مشتق من الفصل بمعنى القطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God instructs people through prophets and their reason in monotheism, good deeds, and warnings, with an implicit threat for disobedience.
rows.anchor: ومن جملة ما فصله للناس الإرشاد إلى التوحيد وصالح الأعمال والإنذار على العصيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: كل شيء is in the accusative after an implied verb that فصلناه explains, with the stated verb occupied by an omitted object pronoun.
rows.anchor: بفعل مضمر يفسره { فصلناه } لاشتغال المذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After encouragement and warning, the passage highlights God’s exhaustive knowledge of deeds, comparing their precise accounting to written records; the specific human deeds follow the general “everything” for emphasis.
rows.anchor: فأعقب ذكر ما فصله الله من الأشياء بالتنبيه على تفصيل أعمال الناس تفصيلا لا يقبل الشك ولا الإخفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every person’s allotted “bird” is the deed God has already determined in His knowledge, which the person inevitably performs in worldly life.
rows.anchor: قدرنا له عمله في علمنا فهو عامل به لا محالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭā’ir can mean an arrow, lot, or marked slip assigning a person a share in a distribution; reports use it for the share allotted by lot.
rows.anchor: أطلق على السهم ، أو القرطاس الذي يعين فيه صاحب الحظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The allotment metaphor may come from drawing named arrows, whose feathering let them pierce the air when shot at divided shares.
rows.anchor: كانوا يرمون السهام المرقومة بأسماء المتقاسمين على صبر الشيء المقسوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it derives from bird omens used especially on journeys; the bird’s sign came to mean a person’s fortune for good or ill.
rows.anchor: من زجر الطير لمعرفة بختت أو شؤم الزاجر من حالة الطير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilzām means making something inseparable, as in the ordinary use of لزمه.
rows.anchor: جعله لازما له ، أي غير مفارق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In his neck” may picture the deed’s closeness as a necklace, since necklaces are worn around the neck.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون كناية عن الملازمة والقرب

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿsha’s verse uses the verb “I put a necklace on it,” illustrating the necklace image.
rows.anchor: والشعر قلدته سلامة ذا فا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may reflect a known practice of hanging marks around people’s necks to designate their duties or status, including a mark used for protected non-Muslims.
rows.anchor: تمثيلا لحالة لعلها كانت معروفة عند العرب وهي وضع علامات تعلق في الرقاب

rows.speaker: بشار
rows.claim: Bashshar’s poem says love was inscribed on his neck like the signet of a protected person, exemplifying neck-marking.
rows.anchor: كتب الحب لها في عنقي موضع الخاتم من أهله الذمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third image is a camel marked on the neck or fitted with a bell so it can be identified and not lost.
rows.anchor: تمثيلا بالبعير الذي يوسم في عنقه بسمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All these images mean that a person receives the full consequence of their good or evil deeds; this differs from the written book described next.
rows.anchor: والمعنى على الجميع أن كل إنسان يعامل بعمله من خير أو شر لا ينقص له منه شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following statement says those deeds will be visibly itemized at resurrection, with nothing small or great omitted from recompense.
rows.anchor: تظهر يوم القيامة مفصلة معينة لا تغادر منها صغيرة ولا كبيرة إلا أحصيت للجزاء عليها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers read ونخرج with the majestic first-person plural and a kasra on rā’; Yaʿqub instead reads the third-person verb referring to God.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور { ونخرج } بنون العظمة وبكسر الراء ، وقرأه يعقوب بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar reads the verb passively with third-person yā’; له is the subject and كتابا its object.
rows.anchor: وقرأه أبو جعفر بياء الغيبة في أوله مبنيا للنائب على أن { له } نائب فاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book records and counts deeds; spreading it is the opposite of folding, and يلقاه means “finds it,” conveying its ready availability.
rows.anchor: والكتاب : ما فيه ذكر الأعمال وإحصاؤها . والنشر : ضد الطي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The open book suggests the person can immediately inspect everything he did, as it arrives already opened for reading.
rows.anchor: والنشر كناية عن سرعة اطلاعه على جميع ما عمله بحيث إن الكتاب يحضر من قبل وصول صاحبه

rows.speaker: ابن عامر، أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Jaʿfar read يُلَقَّاه with passive intensive form, meaning the person is made to receive or encounter the book.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر ، وأبو جعفر { يلقاه بضم الياء وتشديد ، القاف مبنيا للمجهول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unfolding the book means displaying it to be read, as in the verse about the pages being spread.
rows.anchor: ونشر الكتاب إظهاره ليقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Read your book” is direct speech whose omitted speaker is clear from the context.
rows.anchor: مقول قول محذوف دل عليه السياق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative is a compelled challenge that removes their excuse and establishes proof; the person already knows the deeds recorded.
rows.anchor: والأمر في { اقرأ } مستعمل في التسخير ومكنى به عن الإعذار لهم والاحتجاج عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading here means knowing one’s recorded deeds, or understanding miraculous inscriptions if the book has written marks.
rows.anchor: مستعملة في معرفة ما أثبت للإنسان من الأعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bā’ in بنفسك is an added emphatic marker before the subject of كفى, as in the Quranic “God suffices as witness.”
rows.anchor: مزيدة للتأكيد داخلة على فاعل { كفى } كما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥasīban is an accusative specification meaning “reckoner”; عَلَيْكَ implies bearing witness, and the referent is the person from the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: أي من جهة حسيب . والحسيب : فعيل بمعنى فاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sentence explains or unpacks the binding of each person’s fate: guidance benefits its owner and misguidance harms its owner, so the clause is unjoined.
rows.anchor: هذه الجملة بيان أو بدل اشتمال من جملة { وكل إنسان ألزمناه طائره في عنقه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No bearer bears another’s burden” explains why misguidance harms its doer: no one inherits another’s moral benefit or harm.
rows.anchor: واقعة موقع التعليل لمضمون جملة { ومن ضل فإنما يضل عليها }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walid ibn al-Mughira told Quraysh to disbelieve and offered to bear any liability if Muhammad were right, perhaps exploiting people’s hesitation and habits of guarantees.
rows.anchor: كان يقول لقريش : اكفروا بمحمد وعلي أوزاركم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes Walid’s deception and establishes a fundamental rule that one person’s wrongdoing is not charged to another.
rows.anchor: فبين الله للناس إبطال ذلك إنقاذا لهم من الاغترار به

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar related from the Prophet that a dead person is punished because of their family’s wailing.
rows.anchor: عن النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم ( أن الميت ليعذب ببكاء أهله عليه ) قالت عائشة

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha rejected the attribution to the Prophet, invoking the rule that no soul bears another’s burden.
rows.anchor: ما قال رسول الله ذلك والله يقول : { ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At a Jewish woman’s funeral, the Prophet said that her family wept for her while she was being punished.
rows.anchor: ولما مر برسول الله جنازة يهودية يبكي عليها أهلها فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One never bears another’s sin; when someone causes another to sin, the instigator bears their own sin of causing it, not the other person’s transferred burden.
rows.anchor: فإذا كان قد تسبب بوزره في إيقاع غيره في الوزر حمل عليه وزر بوزر غيره لأنه متسبب فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An authentic report says the first son of Adam shares liability in every unjust killing because he first instituted murder.
rows.anchor: ما من نفس تقتل ظلما إلا كان على ابن آدم الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse need not say that one cannot benefit from another’s good deeds, since that does not mislead; such benefit is implied and supported by the prayer to be a model and the report about enduring charity, knowledge, and a righteous child.
rows.anchor: وسكتت الآية عن أن لا ينتفع أحد بصالح عمل غيره اكتفاء إذ لا داعي إلى بيانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blood money paid by a clan for accidental homicide follows a distinct principle of mutual aid, so it does not contradict individual moral responsibility.
rows.anchor: ومن التخليط توهم أن حمل الدية في قتل الخطأ على العاقلة منافف لهذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine “bearer” refers to a soul; the hypothetical statement establishes that even a burdened soul cannot take on another’s burden, so an unburdened soul certainly cannot.
rows.anchor: والوازرة : الحاملة ، وتأنيثها باعتبار أنها نفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wizr is sin likened to a heavy load because it exhausts its bearer in the afterlife, as another verse calls sins burdens.
rows.anchor: والوزر : الإثم لتشبيهه بالحمل الثقيل لما يجره من التعب لصاحبه في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger condition gives full excuse to those astray; it mentions punishment without reward because the point is to remove blame and argument, not to promise favors.
rows.anchor: وهذا استقصاء في الإعذار لأهل الضلال زيادة على نفي مؤاخذتهم بأجرام غيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment most likely means worldly punishment, given the surrounding context and transition to the next verse, though an expansive sense can include both worlds.
rows.anchor: والعذاب هنا عذاب الدنيا بقرينة السياق وقرينة عطف { وإذا أردنا أن نهلك قرية أمرنا مترفيها }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Until” allows the ordinary interval needed for a messenger to preach, people to persist in denial, and punishment to be delayed; the negative participle is general.
rows.anchor: وهذا اتصال عرفي بحسب ما تقتضيه البعثة من مدة للتبليغ والاستمرار على تكذيبهم الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse clearly supports that God mercifully guides people before holding them to account and does not punish a people unreached by His messenger.
rows.anchor: وهي دليل بين على انتفاء مؤاخذة أحد ما لم تبلغه دعوة رسول من الله إلى قوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is a proof for Ashʿarites against Maturidis and Muʿtazilites, who say reason alone obliges recognition of God and leaves no excuse for shirk.
rows.anchor: فهي حجة للأشعري ناهضة على الماتريدي والمعتزلة الذين اتفقوا على إيصال العقل إلى معرفة وجود الله

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilite interpretation that “messenger” means reason strains Arabic and ignores that the verb “send” takes a recipient, not “reason” in this meaning.
rows.anchor: وتأويل المعتزلة أن يراد بالرسول العقل تطوح عن استعمال اللغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse details punishment after messengers, threatens Meccan leaders, and assigns them responsibility for followers they mislead; it also teaches Muslims.
rows.anchor: هذا تفصيل للحكم المتقدم قصد به تهديد قادة المشركين وتحميلهم تبعة ضلال الذين أضلوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although a fā’ might be expected after “We do not punish,” waw makes the warning an independent point; its inferential relation remains clear from context.
rows.anchor: ولكنه عطف بالواو للتنبيه على أنه خبر مقصود لذاته باعتبار ما يتضمنه من التحذير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger brings God’s law, and a people are destroyed when they disobey the commands delivered through that messenger.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أن بعثة الرسول تتضمن أمرا بشرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s intention to destroy is its decisive, operative relation to the event, which takes effect when its causes occur.
rows.anchor: ومعنى إرادة الله إهلاك قرية التعلق التنجيزي لإرادته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We commanded” omits its object: We commanded them to obey what the messenger conveyed, but they disobeyed and acted wickedly.
rows.anchor: أي أمرناهم بما نأمرهم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening إذا makes the syntax seem to place God’s wish to destroy before the wrongdoing, although wrongdoing should cause the punishment and God does not lead people into its cause.
rows.anchor: فيقتضي ذلك أن إرادة الله تتعلق بإهلاك القرية ابتداء فيأمر الله مترفي أهل القرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author resolves the syntax by coordinating “We commanded” with “send a messenger”: after sending and commanding through him, leaders disobey, the threat applies, and God destroys if He wills.
rows.anchor: على لسان الرسول فيفسقوا عن أمرنا فيحق عليهم الوعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destruction is conditional on God’s unconstrained will, as multiple verses affirm.
rows.anchor: أي ذلك بمشيئة الله ولا مكره له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unusual word order inserts a warning that Meccans are exposed to the same fate as earlier peoples who denied messengers.
rows.anchor: وإنما عدل عن نظم الكلام بهذا الأسلوب إلى الأسلوب الذي جاءت به الآية لإدماج التعريض بتهديد أهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among more than eight proposed readings, the closest alternative makes the command clause a description of “town” and leaves the answer to إذا unspoken.
rows.anchor: وأقربها قول من جعل جملة أمرنا مترفيها } إلخ صفة ل { قرية } وجعل جواب ( إذا ) محذوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutraf means given luxury; the wealthy elite were chiefly Meccan polytheists, while most believers then were weak and poor.
rows.anchor: والمترفون هم أهل النعمة وسعة العيش ، وهم معظم أهل الشرك بمكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaders are singled out because they direct the people: when they defy the command, common people follow and corruption spreads through the town.
rows.anchor: فالخطاب في الأكثر يتوجه إليهم ، فإذا فسقوا عن الأمر اتبعهم الدهماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering the ruined generations warns Quraysh that divine punishment has no limit and that delusion prevents people learning from past disasters, especially Noah’s flood.
rows.anchor: ووجه ذكره تذكير المشركين به وأن عذاب الله لا حد له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage turns specifically to the Prophet, assuring him that God knows the people’s sins and will repay them according to their gravity.
rows.anchor: إقبال على خطاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالخصوص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “All-knowing, all-seeing” implies that none of their visible deeds or concealed intentions escapes God; intentions are mentioned first because belief underlies righteous or corrupt action.
rows.anchor: وقدم ما هو متعلق بالضمائر والنوايا لأن العقائد أصل الأعمال في الفساد والصلاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet compared the heart to a morsel of flesh: when sound, the whole body is sound, and when corrupt, the whole body is corrupt.
rows.anchor: إذا صلحت صلح الجسد كله وإذا فسدت فسد الجسد كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Your Lord suffices” suggests the Prophet needs no defender but God, or need not grieve over them, as God told Noah not to ask about what he did not know.
rows.anchor: وفي ذكر فعل ( كفى ) إيماء إلى أن النبي غير محتاج إلى من ينتصر له غير ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The private address to the Prophet indirectly threatens the unbelieving listeners.
rows.anchor: وفي خطاب النبي بذلك تعريض بالوعيد لسامعيه من الكفار
